kernel_of_truth: Eclipse-time gravity anomalies (the Allais effect) are a real, published, and still genuinely unclosed strand of geophysics, not a fabrication. Wang et al. (2000) is a bona fide Phys. Rev. D Rapid Communication, and the Allais / Saxl & Allen lineage does report sub-10 uGal contact-phase anomalies that mainstream geophysics has not fully ruled out. Engaging this literature is not per se pseudoscience, and the dome correctly identifies a real open question.
why_kernel_doesnt_save_claim: Granting the literature is open does not validate WIN-011, because the dome's claim needs three things it does not have: (1) that the SPECIFIC -6.5 uGal value is a real signal — but the original lead observer withdrew it on reanalysis of the same eclipse (Yang & Wang 2002); (2) a predictive rule for WHEN anomalies occur — absent, so an intermittent effect with no stated trigger is unfalsifiable as a 'prediction' and a hit is indistinguishable from cherry-picking; (3) derivation from dome geometry — absent (derives_from_dome=false), the value is adopted post-hoc and then fed into a self-referential kappa check.
intermittency_rebuttal_neutralization: The curmudgeon's advocate (defense_survives=3) said one null (Van Camp, different eclipse) cannot refute an intermittent phenomenon. The reframe makes this objection moot by NOT ruling on the phenomenon: (a) the load-bearing point is a same-eclipse same-author self-retraction, which intermittency cannot touch; (b) a model that uses intermittency to absorb nulls cannot simultaneously bank the one positive as a confirmed prediction without a timing rule; (c) Van Camp is demoted to corroboration. We concede the Allais effect may be a genuine open question and still win on the dome's adopted, retracted, unpredicted number.

proposed_integration_patches.action: Whole-field replacement: reorder to lead with self-retraction, neutralize intermittency rebuttal, add cross-event cherry-pick, demote Van Camp to corroboration.
proposed_integration_patches.find_pattern:
Wang et al. (2000, Phys. Rev. D) used a LaCoste-Romberg D spring gravimeter at Mohe during the 1997 total solar eclipse and reported anomalous gravity 'valleys' of 6–7 μGal at first and last contact — critically, not at eclipse maximum. The dome model’s −6.5 μGal comes from this study. Even granting the dome its preferred value for the sake of argument, the reported timing contradicts the shielding interpretation: the Wang 2000 paper recorded the anomaly at first and last contact — not at eclipse maximum. Gravitational shielding would peak at maximum coverage, not at the contacts. A subsequent reanalysis by the same lead observer (Yang & Wang, 2002, Astrophys. Space Sci. 282, 245–253) found the anomaly evidence weaker once additional measurement controls were applied, and explicitly states ‘no significant anomaly during the very solar eclipse was found.’

Superior instruments found nothing. Van Camp et al. (2001) used four superconducting gravimeters (SGs) — roughly 1,000× more precise than the LaCoste-Romberg — during the 1999 European eclipse and found no eclipse-related gravity signal above the instrument noise floor. When a crude instrument reports a marginal ~2.6σ signal and far superior instruments find nothing, the scientific conclusion is that the original detection was likely an environmental artifact or statistical fluctuation.

The coupling constant is circular. Domain #7 in monitor.py computes κ = 10.9/6.5 = 1.677 nT/μGal, then compares to a hardcoded KAPPA = 1.67 with 5% tolerance. All three values are hardcoded constants — no data is fetched. The 'validation' compares a hardcoded ratio to its own inputs.
proposed_integration_patches.replace_pattern:
The dome's own source withdrew the number. The −6.5 μGal value comes from Wang et al. (2000, Phys. Rev. D), a LaCoste-Romberg D spring-gravimeter reading at Mohe during the 1997 total solar eclipse. But the same lead observer revisited that exact dataset two years later: Yang & Wang (2002, Astrophys. Space Sci. 282, 245–253) applied additional measurement controls and concluded that ‘no significant anomaly during the very solar eclipse was found.’ This is a self-retraction of the specific signal the dome relies on — not a competing measurement of some other event. That distinction carries the whole argument.

Why ‘the effect is intermittent’ cannot rescue it. A dome defender will object that eclipse-gravity (Allais-type) anomalies are reported as intermittent and eclipse-geometry-dependent, so a null at one eclipse cannot refute a positive at another. Granted — but that defense protects the phenomenon, not the dome's use of it. The retraction above is of the same eclipse, the same instrument, the same data, by the same author; intermittency can explain why different eclipses might differ, never why one dataset stops showing a signal on reanalysis. And intermittency cuts both ways: a model that invokes ‘sometimes it appears, sometimes it doesn’t’ to absorb every null forfeits the right to count the one surviving wiggle as a confirmed prediction. The dome states no rule for when an anomaly should occur or how large it should be, so a ‘hit’ is indistinguishable from selecting the single dataset that happened to fluctuate. We are not adjudicating the Allais effect in general — only the dome's adopted, now-retracted, unpredicted number.

The coupling constant is a cross-event cherry-pick validated against itself. Domain #7 in monitor.py computes κ = 10.9 / 6.5 = 1.677 nT/μGal and compares it to a hardcoded KAPPA = 1.67 within a 5% tolerance — a 0.42% ‘agreement’ that is purely self-referential, because the ‘observed’ 1.677 is just the ratio of its own two hardcoded inputs; no gravimeter or magnetometer data is fetched. Worse, those two inputs are not co-measured: the −10.9 nT magnetic value is from the BOU 2017 eclipse (North America, INTERMAGNET), while the −6.5 μGal gravity value is from Mohe 1997 (northeast China, spring gravimeter) — different eclipses, different continents, different instruments, twenty years apart. A genuine ‘coupling’ would be co-measured at one event; this κ stitches together two unrelated numbers and then checks the stitch against itself.

Corroboration from superior instruments. Consistent with the retraction, Van Camp et al. (2001) used four superconducting gravimeters — roughly 1,000× more precise than a LaCoste-Romberg — during the 1999 European eclipse and found no eclipse-related signal above ~0.005 μGal. We present this as supporting context, not as the decisive refutation: the load-bearing point is that the dome's own cited value was withdrawn by its own author and was never tied to a predictive rule, so the claim is unsubstantiated on its own terms — before any different-eclipse null is invoked.
